entries.text: Heating coal without air drives off gases and tar, leaving a carbon-rich solid called coke.
Heating wood without air releases gases and condensable vapours while leaving charcoal. Some chemical energy remains in each stream rather than all becoming heat.
Carbonisation removes most volatile compounds from coal. Reheating the resulting coke yields far less fresh tar because much of that material has already escaped.
Industrial plants can increase hydrogen content by reacting carbon monoxide with steam, forming carbon dioxide too: the water-gas shift reaction.
At high temperature, carbon reacts with steam to form carbon monoxide and hydrogen. The steam is chemically consumed.
Steam reforming breaks down tar compounds into carbon monoxide and hydrogen. These reactions consume heat and commonly use catalysts.
Distillation sorts existing compounds by volatility. Forming chemically different products requires reactions as well; boiling alone cannot explain a change in chemical identity.
Different compounds vaporise and condense at different temperatures. Fractionation collects boiling-range mixtures rather than separating every compound individually.
Cracking breaks large organic molecules into smaller ones. Heavy residues can also leave carbon-rich coke during thermal conversion.
Hydrocarbons react with steam to produce hydrogen and carbon monoxide. Industrial steam reforming commonly uses nickel catalysts and requires heat.
Crushing fractures rock, exposing mineral grains previously locked in surrounding waste rock, called gangue.
Screens separate particles by size; ore grade measures valuable mineral content. These numbered grades track preparation stages, not purity percentages.
Some grains remain locked inside mixed mineral fragments after initial crushing. Further breakage can free them for separation.
Tumbling balls grind ore through impacts and abrasion, freeing mineral grains so later separation can distinguish them from waste.
Beneficiation rejects unwanted minerals to enrich the useful fraction. Concentrates still contain mineral compounds; concentration alone does not make metal.
Reagents change mineral surfaces so selected particles attach to bubbles and rise into froth, while other particles remain in the slurry.
Particles settle through water at different speeds depending on size and density. Hydraulic classifiers exploit this difference to separate them.
Water carries fine waste particles away from retained mineral particles. Washing separates material; chemical extraction of copper is a different operation.
A porous medium retains suspended solids while liquid passes through. This recovers solids from a slurry without requiring a chemical reaction.
Reduction removes oxygen bound in iron oxides. A real process must transfer that oxygen into other products; heating or melting alone does not establish that balance.
Carbon-rich residue from heating coal without air. Coke supplies heat and reducing carbon in ironmaking.
A combustible mixture containing hydrogen, methane and carbon monoxide, released when coal is heated without air.
A mixture rich in hydrogen and carbon monoxide, used as fuel or as feedstock for chemicals such as methanol.
Condensed organic vapours from thermal decomposition. Its many compounds have different boiling ranges, allowing recovery of distinct oil fractions.
Grinding exposes mineral grains by reducing particle size. Fine iron-bearing ore is still mineral material, not iron metal powder.
This preparation chain runs Grade 3 → 2 → 1, then milling. Real ore grade measures valuable mineral content, not stage numbers.
Ore enriched by removing some waste minerals. Iron may still be chemically bound to oxygen until a later reduction step.
Reduction removes oxygen from iron minerals. The resulting metal can still contain impurities; reduction and purification are separate goals.
Waste streams left after mineral separation, often containing water, fine rock, processing chemicals and some unrecovered valuable minerals.
Heating solids without air can decompose them; boiling liquid mixtures can separate compounds by volatility. Feedstock and conditions distinguish chemical conversion from physical separation.
Controlled reactions with steam or oxygen turn carbon-rich feedstock into combustible gas, retaining chemical energy instead of burning everything completely.
Heating separates tar into fractions with different boiling ranges. Lighter fractions vaporise more readily; heavy material remains behind.
Collisions fracture rock and free mineral grains from surrounding gangue. Liberation makes later separation possible.
Surface-active reagents make selected minerals attach to air bubbles. The rising froth carries those particles away from the remaining slurry.
Particles settle at different speeds according to size and density. Controlled water flow turns that difference into a physical separation.
Reduction removes oxygen from metal oxides through chemical reactions. It is distinct from melting, which changes physical state without necessarily changing composition.
Crushing prepares coal physically; carbonisation changes it chemically. Heating without air releases gas and tar while leaving coke, so one feedstock can supply several industrial streams.
Separation and conversion do different jobs. Distillation sorts existing compounds by volatility; cracking breaks molecules apart, while reforming changes their structure or composition.
Ore preparation begins with liberation: breaking rock to free mineral grains. Separation then exploits differences such as density, magnetism or surface chemistry to concentrate useful minerals.

Concentration selects which minerals remain; reduction changes their chemical state; melting changes solid to liquid. Iron oxide must lose oxygen to become iron, even if it has already been finely ground or melted.
These preparation stages advance from Grade 1 through 4 before milling. The numbers are not measured zinc percentages or a universal quality scale.
Buried plant remains become coal through heat and pressure over geological time. Coal combines carbon-rich organic matter with minerals; it is not pure carbon.
When fuel burns, much of its carbon leaves as gas. Mineral matter forms ash, often containing silica and metal oxides rather than the original minerals.
Insoluble organic matter preserved in sedimentary rocks. Heating can break it into smaller hydrocarbons; unlike bitumen, kerogen does not dissolve in organic solvents.
Grinding exposes more surface per unit mass. Fine coal can react faster than large lumps because gases contact more of its surface.
A rock rich in calcium carbonate. Strong heating releases carbon dioxide and leaves calcium oxide, the basis of quicklime.
Making quicklime decomposes calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. The gas comes from the rock itself, not only the furnace fuel.
Soil combines mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and organisms. Its pore spaces store water and allow gases to reach roots.
Sand names a grain-size class, not a single mineral. Quartz is common, but sand can also contain carbonate shell fragments or other minerals.
Washing separates fine clay and silt from coarser grains. It is a physical separation, so the remaining grains keep their mineral identities.
Fungi secrete enzymes into their surroundings and absorb the digested nutrients. Unlike plants, they do not make sugars by photosynthesis.
Spores can disperse and grow into new fungal threads, called hyphae. Unlike a plant seed, a fungal spore contains no embryo.
A fungal substrate supplies organic matter that fungi digest for carbon and energy. Water alone cannot provide the building materials for new biomass.
Plants use light energy to build sugars from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen released by photosynthesis comes from splitting water, not carbon dioxide.
Seeds package a plant embryo with food reserves and a protective coat. Germination draws on those reserves before the seedling can sustain itself.
Early growth draws on seed reserves. As leaves develop, photosynthesis supplies sugars, while roots absorb water and mineral nutrients.
Mosses reproduce with spores rather than seeds and lack the vascular transport system of trees. Fertilisation needs water for sperm to reach the egg.
Plants capture light energy in organic matter. Herbivores and decomposers consume that biomass, transferring carbon and nutrients through an ecosystem.
Plants use carbon dioxide to build sugars, then assemble sugars into cellulose. Much of a tree's dry mass ultimately comes from the air.
Many herbivores rely on gut microbes to digest cellulose in plant cell walls. Microbial fermentation makes this otherwise inaccessible food useful to the animal.
Growing animals need energy and building materials. Digested proteins supply amino acids for making new tissues; food is not just fuel.
In complete insect metamorphosis, egg, larva, pupa and adult are distinct stages. Larvae and adults can occupy different habitats and eat different foods.
In many moths, a caterpillar spins a silk covering around its pupa. The cocoon is that protective covering, not the developing insect itself.
Oxygen lets animal cells extract energy from food, producing carbon dioxide and water. This supports movement and maintenance, even when growth has stopped.
Growth is more than getting bigger: cells divide and specialise into different tissues. Development coordinates those changes into a functioning animal.
A perpendicular force farther from a pivot produces more torque. Mechanical advantage trades force for distance; it does not supply free energy.
Friction-driven conveyors use a pulley to pull the belt. Greater tension and wrap angle increase the traction available before the belt slips.
Borax contains sodium and oxygen as well as boron. Converting it to diborane must account for those other atoms in coproducts, even when they are not listed.
Diborane has two hydrogen bridges between its boron atoms. Each bridge shares one electron pair across three atoms: a three-centre, two-electron bond.
Coal forms geologically; charcoal comes from heating wood without air. Both are carbon-rich fuels, but their origins and mineral impurities differ.
Heating can cause chemical changes before anything melts. Smelting extracts metals through reactions, whereas melting only changes a solid into a liquid.
Compressing an equilibrium gas mixture can favour reactions producing fewer gas molecules. Temperature shifts equilibrium separately, so pressure alone does not determine a furnace's products.
Splitting two water molecules produces two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule. Electrical energy drives this rearrangement; it does not create new atoms.
Salt-water electrolysis produces chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide together. The useful outputs are coupled by the chemistry, rather than being independently selectable products.
An electrolyzer pairs two electrodes with an ion-conducting medium. Electrons travel through an external circuit while ions carry charge internally, connecting the two reaction sites.
An applied voltage can drive a reaction that would not proceed spontaneously. Electrodes exchange electrons with reacting substances, while an electrolyte carries ions between the reaction sites.
Glass lacks a repeating crystal lattice. That disordered structure makes it soften over a temperature range rather than melt at one sharp temperature.
Glass melts become more fluid when heated. Their resistance to flow depends on how easily the connected atomic network can rearrange.
Quartz is crystalline silica. Heating disrupts its ordered arrangement to form a viscous melt; making the final glass also requires controlled cooling.
Cooling a melt without allowing crystals to grow produces glass instead of a crystalline solid. Composition and cooling rate determine whether this happens.
Glassmakers add oxides that modify the atomic network of a melt. Breaking some network links improves fluidity and allows shaping at lower temperatures.
The same elements can form a crystal or a glass. Controlling composition and cooling changes atomic order and therefore properties; glass is not simply a transparent version of quartz.
Dissolved salts provide charged ions that carry electrical current. Their mobility makes brine an electrolyte, unlike the fixed ions in solid salt.
Water-derived hydrogen stores energy supplied during production. Reacting it with oxygen releases energy and forms water; the cycle cannot create energy.
Chlorine gas and chloride in table salt are chemically different. Chloride ions carry an extra electron, which changes their bonding and reactivity.
Current in a magnetic field experiences a force. Motors arrange those forces to produce torque, converting electrical energy into mechanical motion.
Holding a load farther horizontally from a pivot increases its torque. A longer-reaching arm therefore needs greater supporting torque for the same load.
Moving several objects per cycle can raise throughput without faster motion. Larger batches also increase peak loads and may spend longer waiting to be assembled.
Stacking uses vertical space, but taller loads can be less stable during motion. Real handling systems must control sliding and tipping as well as throughput.
Lifting a load takes energy. Lifting the same load through the same height faster requires greater power; real mechanisms also lose energy as heat.
Underground conveyors need continuous belts, supports and drives, abstracted here as paired entrances and exits. Longer routes face belt-strength and drive-power limits.
A splitter redistributes a stream; it cannot multiply the supply. Sustained output is limited by incoming flow, while temporary imbalances require stored material.
Connecting a fast conveyor to a slower receiving machine does not increase that machine's capacity. Transfer points need coordinated rates and somewhere for waiting material.
A production line cannot sustain more output than its limiting stage can supply. Speeding up a different stage may only increase waiting inventory; useful upgrades depend on the whole route.
Throughput depends on objects moved per cycle and the time each cycle takes. Faster arm motion reduces only part of that time: picking, placing and waiting can still limit the rate.

Carrying more objects per cycle can raise throughput without raising cycle frequency. The tradeoff is a larger load per movement, and possibly longer waits while a batch gathers. Capacity and speed are different design choices.

A conveyor can carry more material by moving faster or by carrying more per length of belt. Stacking changes the second quantity; real designs must also accommodate load stability, belt tension and transfer equipment.

Batch production spreads setup effort over several units, but larger lots can increase work in progress and waiting. These recipes change how devices are manufactured, not the device's operating tier.

Buffers absorb short interruptions and timing mismatches between stages; they do not create processing capacity. If average input remains greater than output, the queue continues growing regardless of the transfer equipment's rated speed.
Several devices are made per production batch. In real factories, batching can spread setup costs over more units, but it also ties up material between operations.
Natural boron occurs in compounds such as borate minerals, not as free elemental boron. Major deposits are associated with volcanic activity and dry climates.
Borax commonly contains water within its crystal structure. Losing this water changes the solid itself; it is not simply drying moisture from the surface.
Boric acid is weak, but weak does not mean dilute. Strength describes equilibrium chemistry; concentration describes how much acid is dissolved.
Boron oxide can build a glass network rather than crystallising. Combining it with silica changes glass properties; borosilicate glass is not simply pure silica.
Grinding leaves the chemical formula unchanged but exposes more surface. Finer oxide particles can mix and react more readily than larger lumps.
A mixture combines substances without requiring a chemical reaction. Reacting its components changes chemical identities; simply blending them changes their distribution.
Crystalline boron builds complex networks containing twelve-atom clusters. Its bonding produces a hard solid with semiconducting behaviour, rather than a typical conducting metal.
Boron carbide is used in reactor control rods because boron absorbs neutrons. This affects atomic nuclei, unlike the electron rearrangements in ordinary chemical reactions.
Borate ores can be excavated, while dissolved borates can be recovered from brines. Mining removes material; separation concentrates the useful compounds.
Washing separates useful minerals from unwanted rock and clay. Rejected solids leave with water as sludge; separation changes the mixture, not the number of boron atoms.
Diborane reacts with water to form boric acid and hydrogen gas. Hydrogen is a real coproduct of this reaction, even when only the acid is collected.
Heating boric acid removes water in stages, leaving boron oxide. The released water comes from a chemical transformation, not simply moisture boiling off a wet solid.
Mills produce a range of particle sizes. Classification separates the output so coarse particles can return for further grinding instead of treating every grain as equally fine.
Producing boron alongside diborane couples two outputs. Demand for either product affects how much of the other stream must be used, stored or processed; coproducts are not independently selectable.
This fictional digestive route illustrates element recycling. Organisms redistribute boron rather than create it; recovering the element requires it to have entered through food or mineral inputs.
An element's chemistry depends on its compounds, not just its name. Boron in an oxygen-rich borate behaves differently from boron in a hydride, oxide or carbide; processing connects those forms.

Purity describes chemical composition; particle size describes physical form. A fine powder is not necessarily purer than a coarse solid. Grinding, separation and chemical conversion solve different material-processing problems.
Middle cuts are less volatile than lighter fractions and more volatile than heavier ones. Their composition depends on the feedstock and the chosen collection boundaries.
Octane rating measures resistance to engine knock: unwanted auto-ignition under compression. It is not simply the percentage of octane molecules in the fuel.
Oxygen supports combustion but is not itself a fuel. In many burning reactions it combines with other elements, producing oxides and releasing energy.
Sodium hydroxide dissolves into sodium and hydroxide ions. Hydroxide accepts protons from acids to form water; the remaining ions determine which salt is present.
Rock can combine several minerals, each with its own composition and structure. A rock name therefore does not specify one chemical formula.
Metallic bonding allows iron to deform under pressure rather than immediately shatter. This makes rolling and shaping possible after the metal has been extracted.
Meshing teeth couple rotation. A larger driven gear turns more slowly but delivers greater torque; the exchange cannot increase power, and friction consumes some.
Small amounts of carbon strongly change iron's properties. Steel is an iron-based alloy whose hardness and formability depend on composition and thermal history.
Rotating drums lift grinding media that fall and rub against the feed. Impacts and abrasion break particles, exposing mineral grains for later separation.
Electric current heats resistive conductors. Doubling current quadruples heating at the same resistance; distribution design must consider current as well as connection distance.
Conductivity and strength are different properties. Overhead conductors carry current while supporting their own weight and surviving weather; choosing materials involves several tradeoffs.
Switching, protection and voltage conversion are different jobs. Real substations combine equipment for those functions, linking transmission systems to the networks and loads they serve.
Transformers transfer energy through a changing magnetic field. Their windings and cores still dissipate heat, so changing voltage is not perfectly efficient.
A conductor can connect distant parts of a network without distributing power locally. This waterborne junction provides wire reach rather than a surrounding supply area.
Real fluid flow loses pressure to friction along pipes and at fittings. Required pumping effort depends on flow rate, pipe diameter, roughness and length.
Pipe materials must resist corrosion and mechanical stress. Strength, chemical compatibility and temperature limits are separate requirements; no material is best for every fluid and condition.
Hot pipes expand. Supports and joints must accommodate that movement; constraining it can create stress even when the fluid's pressure is unchanged.
Combustion heat passes through metal walls into water. Boiling absorbs latent heat, so adding energy need not raise temperature while liquid and vapour coexist.
A boiler can receive heat from another system rather than burning fuel locally. The heat source and the water circuit perform different jobs.
Hot exhaust carries energy away. Recovering some of that heat into incoming water can improve fuel use; chemical energy and useful steam output are not identical.
Electrical resistance converts current's energy into heat. This avoids combustion at the boiler, but upstream electricity generation still determines the wider energy and emissions cost.
Heat crosses a separating wall between hot and cold streams without requiring them to mix. Recovering heat can reduce the additional energy needed elsewhere.
More surface area and a larger temperature difference can increase heat transfer. Deposits add thermal resistance, reducing performance even when both fluid streams still flow.
Water absorbs substantial energy for a small temperature rise. Its high specific heat moderates temperature changes and makes it useful for carrying heat.
Steam's energy content is not determined by temperature alone. Pressure and the proportion of liquid droplets also matter, especially near condensation.
Pressurised steam expands and pushes moving parts. A heat engine converts only part of its heat input into work; the rest must be rejected.
Pumps transfer mechanical energy into fluid, raising pressure or elevation. Moving more water against the same pressure difference requires more power; transport does not create energy.
Living systems separate fluids with barriers and controlled exchange. This fictional biofluid conduit follows that principle of dedicated transport rather than serving as an ordinary water pipe.
Metabolism releases heat from food's chemical energy. This fictional animal-powered boiler represents energy conversion; sustained heat output would still require an energy supply.
Water carries heat rather than supplying fuel energy. Combustion produces flue gas; boiling changes water's phase without turning it into carbon-containing exhaust.
Heating raises water's temperature until boiling begins at the prevailing pressure. Further energy then vaporises water rather than necessarily raising its temperature.
Molten salt transfers heat to a separate water stream. Cooling the salt need not consume it chemically; the returning cooler fluid can be heated again.
Geothermal systems extract heat carried by underground fluids. Steam may form through a pressure drop, or a heat exchanger can warm a separate working fluid.
Producing hotter steam requires energy as well as water. A temperature label describes a state, not the source or amount of energy needed to reach it.
Pressure changes water's boiling temperature. Heating and pressurising are different operations; a temperature value alone cannot establish the pressure of an arbitrary steam state.
Transmitting a given power at higher voltage permits lower current. Resistive heating grows with current squared, so this can reduce line losses while demanding more insulation and clearance.

A power network must balance generation and demand while limiting losses and protecting equipment. Bigger conductors, voltage conversion and switching solve different problems; none removes the need to manage current.

Water transports energy through a steam cycle. Pumps add work, boilers add heat, and expansion can produce work. Tracking both energy and material flows prevents treating steam itself as the original fuel.

A thermal power plant converts heat into mechanical work and then electricity. Each stage has losses and operating limits; improving a boiler cannot remove losses in the turbine, generator or electrical network.
Condensing exhaust steam and pumping the liquid back closes a steam cycle. Fuel type changes how heat is supplied; the working-fluid loop still needs heat input, expansion, cooling and circulation.

Useful geothermal power needs heat, a fluid to transport it, and connected pathways through rock. A hot rock deposit alone is not a complete generating system; circulation and heat rejection matter too.

Preservation protects organic material against decay rather than making it metallic. Coal-tar creosote is an industrial wood preservative; durability, strength and electrical insulation remain different material properties.
Preservatives inhibit organisms that degrade wood. Treatment can extend service life, but it does not turn wood into metal or replace electrical insulation.
Coal-tar creosote contains compounds that inhibit wood-destroying organisms. Its toxicity also makes it hazardous to people and other organisms.

Niobium is used mainly as an alloying addition in steels and superalloys. Selecting an alloy requires considering strength, corrosion resistance, operating temperature and manufacturing constraints separately.

Casting uses a mould to shape liquid metal as it freezes. The mould and cooling conditions influence the result; choosing a manufacturing route is separate from deciding how the finished part will be used.

Living systems maintain separate fluid environments with barriers and controlled exchange. This fictional biofluid network illustrates that distinction: the transport medium and its connections are design choices, not simply larger versions of ordinary plumbing.
Graphite's carbon atoms bond strongly within sheets but much more weakly between them. Layers can slide, while mobile electrons also allow electrical conduction.
Steam is superheated when hotter than its saturation temperature at a specified pressure. Higher temperature does not, by itself, mean higher pressure.
Pumps do work to raise water's pressure. Pressurising liquid and vaporising it are different operations; neither creates energy.
Copper can be drawn into long wires without breaking. Thin conductors use less material, but their higher electrical resistance causes more heating at the same current.
Fractional distillation separates mixtures into boiling-range cuts. Lighter fractions vaporise more readily; heavy residues remain after more volatile components have been removed.
Cooling and condensing mixed gases can separate components with different phase-change temperatures. Feed composition and pressure determine what can actually be recovered.
Helium is scarce in air and remains gaseous far below nitrogen's and oxygen's boiling points. Trace-gas recovery requires separation and enrichment, not merely cooling air.
Heating coal with little or no oxygen drives off volatile products while leaving a carbon-rich solid. Recoverable gases and condensed vapours depend strongly on the feed.
Cracking breaks larger organic molecules into smaller ones. Competing reactions can leave carbon-rich coke rather than converting all carbon into lighter liquid or gaseous products.
Hydrocarbons with the same formula can have different atomic arrangements. Branching and ring structures affect combustion behaviour; fuel properties depend on structure, not just carbon content.
Limited oxidation can produce carbon monoxide and hydrogen instead of fully oxidised products. This is chemical conversion, unlike separating compounds that are already present.
Carbon monoxide reacts with water to form carbon dioxide and hydrogen. This increases hydrogen content through a chemical reaction, not a boiling-point separation.
Tar recovery from rock requires carbon-bearing organic matter. Ordinary silicate minerals and water do not provide the carbon needed to make an organic tar.
A slurry suspends solid particles in a liquid. Separating the solids changes the mixture, whereas producing different organic molecules requires chemical conversion.
Biomass pyrolysis yields char, gases and condensable vapours. Condensed bio-oil can undergo further conversion, but geological coal formation is a different, much slower process.
Oxidising anthracene can form anthraquinone's carbonyl groups. This changes chemical structure; sorting a mixture by boiling point cannot supply the required oxygen atoms.

Solvents dissolve different substances to different extents. Polarity and molecular interactions influence which components dissolve, helping separate materials without changing their chemical identities.
Heating urea can release ammonia and isocyanic acid as early products. Further reactions compete, so decomposition is a network of reactions rather than one universal clean split.
The cumene process oxidises cumene, then splits an intermediate into phenol and acetone. These are coupled reaction products, not substances obtained by simply boiling pure cumene.
Tall oil is recovered from wood-pulping liquors and contains fatty and resin acids. Its name does not mean crude petroleum or arbitrary tar, and it is not a single chemical.

Polymers are built from repeating molecular units. Different monomers and bonding arrangements give different properties; a generic plastic product leaves the actual polymer and its synthesis unspecified.
Lignin is a complex aromatic polymer. Breaking it down can yield mixtures of phenolic compounds; obtaining one purified chemical requires additional selectivity and separation.
Latex contains tiny rubber particles dispersed in water. Acid can destabilise the dispersion so particles gather into a solid mass; this is coagulation, not distillation.
Oxidising titanium tetrachloride produces titanium dioxide and releases chlorine. Recovering chlorine lets it serve again in upstream chlorination; recycling a reagent is different from creating it.
Combining different monomers can make a copolymer whose properties differ from either homopolymer. Composition and chain structure matter more than treating all acrylic materials as interchangeable.
Cooling coal-pyrolysis vapours condenses some compounds into tar. Others remain gaseous; changing temperature affects recovery without making all components share one boiling point.
Coal contains organic matter and minerals. Heating releases gases and vapours while leaving mineral-rich residues; a solid byproduct is not necessarily newly formed carbon.
Breaking lignin yields many phenolic compounds. Selectivity measures how much reaction favours the desired product; isolating pure phenol also requires separation from chemically similar byproducts.
A changing current creates a changing magnetic field, which induces a voltage opposing that change. Inductors store magnetic energy; they do not simply block all current.
A capacitor stores energy in an electric field between separated conductors. Capacitance depends on geometry and dielectric material; it is distinct from the maximum permitted voltage.
A resistor limits current and dissipates heat. Resistance and power rating are different specifications; higher tiers do not necessarily mean greater resistance or wattage.
Heating a cathode releases electrons into a vacuum. Other electrodes collect or control that flow, allowing a tube to rectify or amplify electrical signals.
Transistors use one electrical signal to control another current. Amplification needs a power supply; the control signal does not create the output energy.
A semiconductor junction conducts much more readily in one direction than the other. This allows rectification: converting alternating current into a one-direction flow.
Many electronic devices and their interconnections can be fabricated on one substrate. Integration shortens connections, but power consumption and heat removal remain design constraints.
Resistance changes with temperature as charge transport changes. Stable resistors minimise unwanted drift; the paradiagmatic name supplies no temperature coefficient.
In a light-emitting diode, electrons and holes recombine to emit photons. The semiconductor's energy gap influences colour; CSLE is a game-specific designation.
Inductors oppose rapid current changes by storing magnetic energy. Fault-current limiting protects equipment, but its performance depends on the circuit and magnetic material.
Porous electrodes expose enormous internal surface area. Charge separation at the electrode-electrolyte interface stores energy, unlike a battery's bulk chemical energy storage.
A Josephson junction carries supercurrent across a weak link. A pi junction favours a half-cycle phase difference between superconductors, not a classical voltage offset.
Conductive tracks on an insulating substrate connect components. The board provides wiring and mechanical support; mounted components supply the circuit's other functions.
Connections determine circuit behaviour, not merely the parts list. The same components can perform different tasks when arranged into different networks.
Many ceramics resist heat and conduct electricity poorly. Their strong bonding can also make them brittle; electrical insulation does not imply resistance to cracks or impact.
Paper or fibre layers reinforce a resin binder. Pressing and curing unite the layers into a composite; the resulting properties depend on both reinforcement and resin.
Cellulose fibres reinforce plant cell walls. In wood, lignin binds those fibres together; chemical pulping separates them by dissolving much of the surrounding lignin.
Electrode reactions drive electrons through an external circuit. Ions carry charge through the electrolyte; chemical changes provide energy rather than create charge.
Electronic parts use conductors, insulators and semiconductors to control charge. Making individual devices and connecting them into working circuits require different manufacturing operations.
Placement machines position components on circuit boards. Soldering then forms electrical and mechanical joints; accurate placement alone does not create a reliable connection.
Circuit boards combine insulating substrates with patterned conductors. Layers, holes and connections define the board's structure; fabrication is separate from mounting electronic components.
Chemical pulping separates cellulose fibres by dissolving much of the lignin that binds wood together. Washing and chemical recovery are separate operations from producing the fibres.
Screens divide particles by whether they pass through an opening. Size separation can assist mineral recovery, but the screen does not directly identify a particle's chemical composition.
Copper-bearing minerals occur mixed with other rock. Mineral composition determines the extraction route; an ore is neither pure metal nor a single fixed compound.
Mobile electrons carry current and transfer heat through copper. High conductivity makes it useful for wiring and heat transfer, but resistance still produces losses.
Grade 1 is crushed into Grade 2; screening then advances toward Grades 3 and 4. These are preparation stages, not measured copper percentages.
Fine particles expose more surface area but are harder to recover selectively. Excessive grinding can send valuable mineral grains into waste streams.
Rejected material can still contain valuable mineral. Recrushing may liberate it from gangue, but extra recovery costs energy, wear and additional separation.
Grade describes valuable-material concentration; recovery describes the fraction retrieved from the feed. A high-grade product can still leave metal behind in waste.
Enrichment raises the valuable-mineral content. A concentrate can still contain compounds and impurities; concentration and chemical reduction are separate operations.
Reduction can turn copper ions into metal by supplying electrons. Purity is a separate measurement; a recipe does not verify the 99.9% label.
Heating bonds particles without fully melting the mass. The result can retain pores; sintering improves cohesion but does not by itself establish chemical purity.
Mineral pulps suspend particles in liquid. Successive treatment stages change the mixture; a stage number is neither a molecular formula nor a purity measurement.
Leaching moves copper from minerals into dissolved chemical species. Dissolution is not the same as melting; dissolved copper still needs recovery from the liquid.
A pregnant solution is loaded with dissolved valuable material. The term describes process status, not a new compound or proof that impurities are absent.
Melting requires energy to change solid metal into liquid, beyond raising its temperature. Cooling releases this latent heat again as the metal solidifies.
Screens sort particles by size, not chemistry. Enrichment is possible when composition correlates with size, but a finer fraction is not automatically purer copper.
Crushing can free valuable mineral grains from surrounding rock. It changes particle size and accessibility, not copper atoms; later separation decides which fragments are recovered.
Particles settle at different rates depending on size, density and shape. Fluid classification exploits those differences; it is not a chemical test of every passing grain.
Precipitation forms solid compounds from a solution; electrowinning deposits metal using electric current. These are distinct recovery routes, not consequences of stirring alone.
Copper extraction can require changing copper's oxidation state. Reducing agents supply electrons and are themselves oxidised; heat alone does not balance the chemical reaction.
Sintering improves cohesion by joining particles before complete melting. Temperature, time and atmosphere control bond growth and porosity; more heat does not simply mean purer metal.
Fluxes help impurities enter a separate slag phase. Melting makes a liquid; refining depends on which substances transfer into slag, gas or another phase.
Molten metal takes the shape of a mould as it solidifies. Cooling conditions influence grain structure and defects; casting changes shape but does not purify the metal.
Smelting extracts metal through chemical reactions, while melting only changes physical state. The extraction route depends on whether copper occurs as oxides, sulfides or native metal.
Leaching dissolves components from solid feed; later stages recover them from solution. Solvent choice and mineral chemistry determine selectivity, not the number attached to a pulp stream.

Copper extraction combines liberation, separation and chemical conversion. Improvements must consider both recovery and final purity: increasing one stream's grade can leave more valuable metal in another.

Resistors dissipate energy; capacitors and inductors store it temporarily. Active devices control currents using power from a supply. Circuit design chooses connections and operating ranges, not just a collection of components.

Small dopant concentrations change the number and type of mobile charge carriers in a semiconductor. N-type and p-type identify the majority carriers: electrons or holes, not negatively or positively charged bulk chunks.

Increasing throughput must preserve process control: more components per minute still need consistent material properties, geometry and connections. Faster equipment does not change the electrical principles of the devices it makes.

Ceramic performance depends on composition, bonding and microstructure. Electrical insulation, heat resistance and mechanical toughness are different properties; improving one does not automatically improve all of them.

Some superconducting devices use phase differences across weak links to control current. Their behaviour follows quantum mechanics; a materials list alone cannot establish whether a circuit performs quantum computation.
Capacitance alone does not measure energy capacity. Stored energy also depends on operating voltage; delivering high power and storing a large amount of energy are different design objectives.

Throughput depends on the slowest stage, not just the speed of each machine. Feed preparation, processing and separation must be matched; faster equipment elsewhere cannot remove an unchanged bottleneck.
A useful solvent need not dissolve everything. Differences in molecular interactions let one component enter a liquid while another remains behind; selecting the solvent helps control separation.

A colloid can remain dispersed even though its particles are not dissolved molecules. Changing surface interactions can destabilise it, allowing a dispersed polymer to gather into a recoverable solid.

Wood combines cellulose-rich fibres with lignin and other constituents. Separating these fractions creates distinct feedstocks: recovering fibres and converting aromatic lignin solve different chemical problems.

Polymer properties depend on monomers, chain structure and composition. A generic plastic label hides these differences; replacing one polymer with another can change stiffness, heat resistance and chemical compatibility.

Gases have different condensation and boiling temperatures, which depend on pressure. Cryogenic separation exploits those differences, but trace components still need enrichment; low temperature does not imply a pure product.
